summary: The paper studies a drop-and-refit filter: fit logistic regression with 5-fold cross-validation on noisy labels, drop samples whose out-of-fold prediction disagrees with the label, and refit. On digits and breast cancer (scikit-learn) with symmetric noise at 20% and 40%, and 5 seeds, dropped samples are about 71% truly flipped, the refit model beats plain logistic regression in most cells and an untuned MLP in all noisy cells, and it costs a small amount on clean labels. The authors state the scope is small and make no claim beyond it.
strengths: Scope is stated plainly and repeatedly (two small datasets, symmetric noise, no deep networks), and the abstract and discussion do not claim more than the experiments show.

The mechanism is measured directly with precision and recall of the dropped set against the known flips, not only through downstream accuracy. Per-seed paired comparisons with shared splits, noise draws and folds are the right design for the question.

Unfavorable results are reported: the high-noise breast-cancer cell (sd about 9 points, only 22% of the loss recovered), a non-significant low-noise breast-cancer gain, the clean-label cost, and the roughly 5x fit time. Fig. 2 shows individual seeds.
The method is simple, has no hyperparameters beyond K, and is easy to reproduce.

weaknesses.issue: The headline comparison against the MLP is not a meaningful test of the filter. The MLP is untuned, has no early stopping or regularization, and is not a noise-robust method. Its collapse under noise (65% on both datasets at 40%) is the expected behavior of an overfitting model, and the paper itself says it did not test that explanation. The sentence 'beats an MLP in every run' in the abstract and contribution list therefore says little about the value of filtering.
weaknesses.where: Abstract; Sec. 1 contributions; Sec. 4.3; Table 1; Fig. 2
weaknesses.suggestion: Add the controls the authors can run cheaply: the same MLP trained on the filtered set (filter then MLP), and an MLP with early stopping or weight decay. Otherwise cut the MLP claim from the abstract and contribution list and present the MLP only as a reference point.

weaknesses.issue: No competing noise-handling baseline. The text frames the work against confident learning and Brodley and Friedl's filters, yet the closest method, confident learning (which uses the same out-of-fold probabilities), is not run. The method is the Brodley and Friedl single-algorithm filter with logistic regression, so the novelty is the measurement. Without a comparison, the reader cannot tell whether the simple rule is adequate or whether thresholds and per-class counts matter.
weaknesses.where: Sec. 1 paragraph 3; Sec. 3 last sentence of 'Why' paragraph; Sec. 4 'Models'; Sec. 6
weaknesses.suggestion: Run confident learning (cleanlab's find_label_issues on the same out-of-fold probabilities) and a majority-vote or probability-threshold variant on the same splits and add them to Tables 1 and 2. If that is impossible, state in the abstract that the contribution is an empirical check of a known filter, not a new method.

weaknesses.issue: The precision test is against the wrong null. The one-sample t-test compares precision with 50%, labeled 'chance', but a filter that dropped samples at random would have precision equal to the noise rate (20% or 40%), and at 20% noise a precision of 65% is much better than 50% suggests. More informative would be enrichment over the base rate. Pooled precision (71%) mixes settings with different base rates and sample sizes and is hard to interpret. The claim that 'most dropped samples are truly flipped' is true, but the p-values add little.
weaknesses.where: Sec. 4 'Metrics and statistics'; Sec. 5.1; Table 2 'p vs 50%'; Abstract
weaknesses.suggestion: Report precision relative to the realized noise rate (lift, or a test against it), and drop or justify the 50% null and the pooled figure. Report per-setting precision with the drop fraction next to it.

weaknesses.issue: Statistical support is thin and the claims drift past it. With 5 seeds, t-tests on paired differences are fragile, and about a dozen tests are run with no multiplicity correction. The 'trend test' for gain versus noise is not described. The abstract says 'all but one paired noisy run', the intro says 'every noisy setting we ran', and Sec. 5 says 'five of six cells' (which counts the clean cells inconsistently). The breast-cancer 40% cell has a gain of 3.6 points with sd about 9 and recall of 79%, yet it is counted as support.
weaknesses.where: Abstract; Sec. 1 paragraph 4 ('every noisy setting'); Sec. 5 opening ('five of six dataset-noise cells'); Sec. 5.2
weaknesses.suggestion: Use one consistent wording tied to the table. Describe the trend test in a sentence. Increase to 20 or more seeds (the data are tiny and cheap) or switch to repeated splits. Note the multiplicity or use a nonparametric paired test. Soften 'in every noisy setting' for breast cancer at high noise, where only 22% of the loss is regained.

weaknesses.issue: The evidence base is too narrow for the framing. Digits is close to linearly separable, so a linear out-of-fold model is nearly the ideal detector, and breast cancer is binary, where symmetric 40% noise leaves almost no signal. Both are tiny, and no class-dependent or instance-dependent noise is tested, even though real flips are rarely symmetric and a linear model will systematically misclassify hard classes (these would be dropped as 'flipped'). The clean-label drops (3.5% on digits, 1.9% on breast cancer) show that hard clean samples are removed, and no analysis shows whether dropped clean samples concentrate on confusable classes, which would bias the refit model.
weaknesses.suggestion: Add at least one harder dataset (e.g. a CIFAR-10 or fashion-MNIST subset on frozen features, which stays in the linear setting), and one asymmetric noise setting. Add a per-class breakdown of dropped clean samples on digits.

weaknesses.issue: Method argument is untested and the design is unablated. The 'Why disagreement marks a flipped label' paragraph concedes that no experiment tests it. The choice K=5, C=1, and a single pass are not varied, and with 40% noise the out-of-fold models are trained on heavily corrupted labels, so recall may depend strongly on C and K. Iterated filtering and the effect of regularization are obvious questions. The reported 'recovered share' is the authors' own metric and is unstable when the denominator (the loss from noise) is small.
weaknesses.suggestion: Add a small sensitivity table for K in {3,5,10} and C in {0.01,1,100}, and one iterated-filter variant. Report the recovered share with its per-seed spread or drop it in favor of accuracy gain.

weaknesses.issue: The 'honest account' contribution and the sentence about recomputing all numbers with the Scriptorium pipeline are not scientific contributions. The sentence in Sec. 3 about the pipeline is out of place in a method section, and the third bullet describes the paper's tone, not a result.
weaknesses.where: Sec. 1 third bullet; Sec. 3 final paragraph
weaknesses.suggestion: Replace the third bullet with a concrete finding (for example, the clean-label cost and the cost-versus-noise tradeoff) and move reproducibility to a footnote or the code statement.

weaknesses.issue: Minor reporting gaps. Compute time is 'indicative, machine unknown'. The test sets are small (171 samples for breast cancer, so one sample is 0.6 points), which sits in the same range as the effects. The MLP seed varies together with the split, so the MLP variance mixes both sources. The title (long, with a claim that 'finds the flipped labels') overstates the 79% recall on breast cancer at high noise.
weaknesses.suggestion: Report the hardware, say how test-set size limits resolution, and shorten the title to what is shown.

questions: How does the filter compare to confident learning on the same splits, and to the filter followed by an MLP?
Does recall on breast cancer at 40% fall because the out-of-fold model is trained on too many flipped labels? How do K and C change it?
Which classes do the dropped clean digits come from, and does the refit model lose accuracy on them?
Why is 50% the null for precision rather than the realized noise rate?
Do the conclusions hold with 20 or more seeds, given the sd of about 9 points in one cell?
